summary: Summarizes the requirements the SPKI working group drew up for certificates, based on a list of things one might want to do with them. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A wish list for digital ID cards, boiled down to what they must do.

questions: why not name to key certificates
subtitle: What the SPKI working group wanted from certificates: permissions first, names second, and as simple as possible.

tldr.problem: Traditional certificates bind a name to a key, but a person's name is rarely what a security decision needs. What a verifier needs to know is whether a keyholder has been granted a specific authorization.
tldr.mechanism: The SPKI working group collected a brainstorming list of things people might want certificates for and summarized it into requirements: authorization-centred, minimal, simple to encode, able to carry validity dates and revocation in a deterministic way.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an Experimental requirements document, not a protocol. It states what an SPKI certificate should do and leaves the format to other work.

today: RFC 2692 is an Experimental requirements memo. It is not an Internet standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Charter and Purpose
sections.content:
The IETF Simple Public Key Infrastructure (SPKI) working group was tasked with producing a certificate structure and operating procedure for trust management that is as easy, simple and extensible as possible. The charter calls for an IETF-sponsored public key certificate format, associated signature and other formats, and key acquisition protocols, all simple to understand, implement and use.

The group first listed things one might want to do with certificates, then summarized that list into requirements. This memo presents the summary, with the list attached at the end. The charter names IPSEC protocols, encrypted electronic mail, WWW documents and payment protocols as intended users, and says SPKI should support a range of trust models.
sections.plainLanguage: A group of people wrote down what a simple digital permission slip should be able to do, starting from a long list of ideas.

sections.title: Why Not Name-to-Key Certificates
sections.content:
The word certificate goes back to Loren Kohnfelder's MIT bachelor's thesis, which answered a suggestion by Diffie and Hellman. They had proposed a modified telephone book with public keys in place of telephone numbers. Kohnfelder noted that an on-line directory is a performance bottleneck and proposed digitally signed directory entries instead. Since 1978 the term has often been taken to mean a binding between a name and a key.

The SPKI team concluded that such <name,key> bindings are of extremely limited use for trust management. A name is one attribute of a keyholder, and it is rarely of security interest. A certificate user needs to know whether the keyholder has been granted some specific authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: Knowing someone's name does not tell you if they are allowed through the door. SPKI cares about the permission, not the name.

sections.title: General Requirements
sections.content:
A keyholder is the person or other entity that controls the private key matching a public key. The main purpose of an SPKI certificate is to authorize an action, give permission or grant a capability to or for a keyholder. The keyholder is most directly identified by the key itself, though a collision-free hash of the key or a name to be resolved later may be used as an indirection.

  • New authorizations are defined by the author of the code that uses the certificate, with no need to ask any other person or organization.
  • Certificates are assumed to be handed directly by the keyholder to the verifier, since they may carry information the keyholder does not want published. Use of a global repository such as LDAP, the global PGP key server or DNS is the keyholder's choice.
  • Each certificate should carry the minimum information needed, like a single key rather than a key ring, so the dossier of all one's certificates does not become a privacy violation.
  • Some certificates must be anonymous: a certificate must be able to assign an attribute to a blinded signature key, as needed in secret balloting.
  • A certificate must be able to bind a key to names, and if possible SPKI should support the SDSI name construct of Rivest and Lampson. The memo notes that SPKI and SDSI have merged.
sections.plainLanguage: A permission slip should say only what is needed, be made by whoever owns the thing, and be handed over by you, not posted for everyone to see.

sections.title: Validity and Revocation
sections.content:
An SPKI certificate should be able to carry a validity period of dates. It may also need on-line refinement of validity, which earlier designs achieved with a Certificate Revocation List (CRL). A minimal CRL holds uniquely identified revoked certificates, a sequence number and a signature; a CRL annihilates any listed certificate and any earlier CRL. The memo says this leads to non-deterministic program behavior.

So the requirement is that, if SPKI uses CRLs, the certificate must tell the verifier where to find the CRL, the CRL must carry explicit validity dates, and the dates of a sequence of CRLs must not overlap. Validation is then deterministic, aside from clock skew.

The memo calls a CRL a negative statement, like the paper books of bad checks given to cashiers, and notes retail moved to positive on-line validation. SPKI should support both positive and negative on-line validations. Every CRL or revalidation instrument needs its own lifetime, and a lifetime of 0 is not possible because of communication delays and clock skew.
sections.plainLanguage: A permission slip needs an expiry date. A list of cancelled slips must say when it is valid, so everyone reaches the same answer.

sections.title: Keeping Certificates Simple to Build
sections.content:
Certificates should be generated by any keyholder empowered to grant or delegate the authorization, with code written by many developers, often working alone. They should also be usable in constrained environments such as smart cards or small embedded systems, so code and memory should be as small as possible.

  • A bare minimum of fields and an absolute minimum of optional fields; the structure should constrain the creator, not the reader's error messages.
  • A description that relates directly to structures a C or PASCAL programmer would write. No library code should be required to pack or parse, and ASN.1 is not to be used.
  • A certificate is signed exactly as transmitted, with no reformatting before checking the signature, though white space might be canonicalized on input for a text format.
  • If possible, an LR(0) grammar, so data is read once into a usable structure, and packing and parsing without recursion.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone, even a hobbyist, should be able to make and read these slips with a tiny program, so they must be plain and short.

sections.title: The List of Certificate Uses
sections.content:
The attached list is a brainstorming list from the SPKI mailing list. It runs from permission to write electronic checks, bank-to-bank certificate chains and security clearances, to assurance about downloaded software, a "reputation voucher" for a friend, and wallet cards turned into certificates such as a driver's license, health insurance card or membership card.

It also separates three kinds of name binding: a traditional certificate binding a key to a unique person, a direct certificate where a key declares the name it goes by in a self-signed certificate, and a personal binding of a key to a nickname for private use.

An Open Questions section answers hard cases. Private key theft or misuse is a matter of key protection that certificate format cannot prove. A house title scan needs a database that is unrelated to certificate structure. A certificate saying "not already married" would need an organization able to determine that fact, and the method is not part of the certificate definition. The memo's Security Considerations say only that security issues are discussed throughout.
sections.plainLanguage: The list shows lots of everyday cards, like library or club cards, that could become digital permission slips. The memo also admits some questions have no certificate answer.
